name: journal-paul-pharisee-or-sadducee.json
content:
Was Paul a Pharisee or a Sadducee? A Pharisee, on his own word. He says so in a letter and again before a council, and no source calls him anything else. The harder question is what kind of Pharisee he was, because the man who claims the name spent his persecuting years in the service of the Sadducees.

Paul names the party once in his own hand. In the list of his credentials he writes "Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee."1 In Galatians he says he outran his equals in "the Jews' religion", "being more exceedingly zealous of the traditions of my fathers."2 That verse never uses the word Pharisee, but the traditions are the giveaway. Josephus says the Pharisees handed the people many observances from their fathers that are not written in the law of Moses, and that the Sadducees reject them for that reason.3

[paulus_figure name="qumran-caves-judean-desert-cliffs-7161376"]The caves at Qumran above the Dead Sea, where a library of Jewish scrolls was found. Paul's Judaism was one of several in his day.[/paulus_figure]

Acts says it twice more. Before Agrippa, Paul says "after the most straitest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee."4 In Jerusalem he says he was "brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel."5 Luke has already told us that Gamaliel was "a Pharisee, named Gamaliel, a doctor of the law, had in reputation among all the people."6 Only Acts gives Paul a Pharisee father. His letters name no parent at all.

The line that matters most comes before the council. Paul "perceived that the one part were Sadducees, and the other Pharisees," and he cried out, "Men and brethren, I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee: of the hope and resurrection of the dead I am called in question."7 The council split on the spot. "For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, neither angel, nor spirit: but the Pharisees confess both."8 The scribes of the Pharisees' party then rose and said, "We find no evil in this man: but if a spirit or an angel hath spoken to him, let us not fight against God."9

[paulus_figure name="ancient-stone-seats-amphitheatre-emp-33678797"]Tiered stone seats in the ruins of an ancient theatre. Paul spoke to a divided council (Acts 23:6–9).[/paulus_figure]

The title bought him protection, and he used it again before Felix: "Touching the resurrection of the dead I am called in question by you this day."10 Look at what he did there. The Pharisees believed in a resurrection of the dead at the end, and Paul agreed with them. What he preached was larger: one man had already risen, and that man was Lord. The council that divided over the first belief never weighed the second.

[paulus_figure name="rock-cut-tomb-entrance-stone-38072625"]The entrance of an ancient rock-cut tomb. Whether the dead rise was the line between the Pharisees and the Sadducees.[/paulus_figure]

Now the awkward part. The Pharisee who claims the name worked for the Sadducee high priest. When the apostles were jailed, Acts says the high priest and "all they that were with him" were "the sect of the Sadducees."11 Saul "went unto the high priest, And desired of him letters to Damascus to the synagogues, that if he found any of this way, whether they were men or women, he might bring them bound unto Jerusalem."12 Meanwhile the one Pharisee Luke names, Gamaliel, told the same council to leave the apostles alone: "if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought: But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it."13

So the pupil of the Pharisee who urged restraint became the agent of the party that wanted the followers of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (ʿalayhi al-salām, peace be upon him) silenced. Luke does not explain it, and I doubt that anyone can from Acts alone. A man trained among the Pharisees could have served the temple authorities for his own reasons. Or the title was worth more to him in a council chamber than it was in his conduct. I read it the second way, and the evidence allows the first.

Either way, nothing makes him a Sadducee. What remains is a man who names the right party at the right moment. In Philippians the name outranks his rivals' credentials. In Jerusalem it splits a council. The claim does a job each time, and [paulus_link slug="saul-the-persecutor" /] asks what job it did when he held the high priest's letters.

One more fact belongs here. ʿĪsā ibn Maryam spoke harshly to the Pharisees by name: "woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!"14 Paul chose to describe himself, years after his call, by the name of the party his Lord had rebuked. He never says why. His handling of the Tanakh is the next thing to test, and [paulus_link slug="borrowings-from-the-rabbis" /] and [paulus_link slug="typology" /] do it.

Was Paul a Pharisee or a Sadducee? Questions readers ask

Was Paul a Pharisee?

Yes, by his own account: "as touching the law, a Pharisee" (Philippians 3:5), and "I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee" (Acts 23:6). He says it in a letter and again in speeches that Luke reports.

Was Paul ever a Sadducee?

No source says so. He did serve the Sadducee high priest as an agent against the followers of ʿĪsā (Acts 9:1–2), but acting for a party is different from belonging to it.

What is the difference between a Pharisee and a Sadducee?

The Pharisees affirmed the resurrection, angels and spirits, and kept the traditions of the fathers. The Sadducees denied the resurrection and held to the written law alone (Acts 23:8; Josephus, Antiquities 13.297; 18.12–17).

Was Paul still a Pharisee after he became a follower of Christ?

Acts has him say "I am a Pharisee" in the present tense, years after his call (Acts 23:6). Philippians puts the same claim in the past, among the things he says he counted as loss (Philippians 3:5–7).
